topics.title: 26.2.1 Stopping Admission Before Releasing Resources
topics.summary: A drain begins by preventing new work from entering the lifecycle being stopped. Then already admitted work either completes within a budget or receives a defined interruption outcome. Finally the owner joins background activity and destroys shared state.

topics.title: 26.3.2 Defining Rollback Conditions Before Deployment
topics.summary: Rollback must consider state written by the new version. If the old binary cannot read that state, replacing the executable is not enough. A forward fix, compatible reader, or data recovery procedure may be required.

cards.question: Explain Defining Rollback Conditions Before Deployment in your own words.
cards.answer: Rollback must consider state written by the new version. If the old binary cannot read that state, replacing the executable is not enough. A forward fix, compatible reader, or data recovery procedure may be required.

reading.title: 26.3.2 Defining Rollback Conditions Before Deployment
paragraphs: Rollback must consider state written by the new version. If the old binary cannot read that state, replacing the executable is not enough. A forward fix, compatible reader, or data recovery procedure may be required.

Define observable abort conditions: elevated error categories, growing backlog age, unexpected schema rejection, resource exhaustion, or violated invariants. Tie them to a specific deployment revision. A rollout should not continue merely because aggregate CPU remains low.

reading.title: Engineering case — Stop a gateway while accepted work remains pending
paragraphs: The worker is unavailable and the gateway has accepted five jobs. An operator needs to replace the gateway binary. Waiting for every job to complete would block indefinitely; exiting without preserving state would lose obligations.

The supported lab transition stops admission, terminates the gateway through its normal signal path, joins the dispatcher, and retains the gateway database. The next process opens the same file and resumes selecting pending jobs. Completion is deferred, but acceptance remains represented durably.

A client can lose its response during this transition. On reconnect, it reuses the same key or queries status. The gateway’s duplicate contract remains essential during deployment, not just during network incidents. Creating a new key after every restart would turn an operational transition into additional business work.

The worker file must also be retained. If a worker completed one of the jobs before the outage, its receipt resolves a later replay. Replacing the gateway does not authorize resetting the worker’s state or copying it into several independent authorities.

Now consider a new binary that requires schema version 2. The maintenance procedure must run a supported migration and verify rollback compatibility. Simply keeping the file is not enough if the replacement code cannot interpret it. Deployment state and schema state are coupled through the accepted-work contract.

A useful smoke test after restart checks more than PING: inspect one prior completed key, one prior pending key, an identical duplicate, a conflicting duplicate, and a new key. Then restore the worker and observe pending completion. These checks target continuity of meaning across the transition.

The test does not prove zero downtime or orchestration integration. It proves a controlled local replacement path with retained state under the specified environment. That narrower evidence is valuable because an operator can reproduce it and know exactly what it supports.
